ch15.anchor: the way toward the Red River bridge
ch15.note: The great cantilever bridge over the Red (Hong) River at Hanoi, opened in 1902 and long known as the Pont Doumer, after Paul Doumer, the governor-general who had it built; today it is the Long Bien Bridge. Carrying road and rail on a single narrow deck, and here under repair so that traffic crossed one lane at a time, it is the bottleneck on which the car chase turns.

The source spells this operative's surname 'Chen' here in Chapter Five, and so does the Biography of Dai Yunong quoted later in the chapter; but in Chapter Three it was written 'Zheng.' He is one and the same man, and one of the three of the team captured at Hanoi. He is rendered 'Chen Bangguo' throughout this translation, following the fuller and semi-official usage; the discrepancy is the source's own.

A hill resort some hours north of Hanoi. Chen calls it Da Le; the Biography of Dai Yunong quoted below calls the same place Dan Dao, and the Wang-regime memoir calls it San Tao Shan. The three names are not reconciled in the sources, and the exact identification of the resort is uncertain.

ch15.anchor: The Secret Records of President Chiang
ch15.note: Jiang zongtong milu: a large semi-official life of Chiang Kai-shek serialized by the Sankei Shimbun of Japan and compiled from materials supplied by the Nationalist Party History Committee. It is a real work; its account of the Hanoi killing, quoted here, agrees in the main with Chen's own, including the detail that Wang had changed rooms that night.

ch15.anchor: The Biography of Mr. Dai Yunong
ch15.note: Dai Yunong xiansheng zhuan: the 1979 life of Dai Li published by the Intelligence Bureau of the Ministry of National Defense in Taiwan, a real and semi-official work drawn from the service's own archives. Chen treats its account as carrying the weight of an official record, while noting where it differs from his memory.

ch15.anchor: The Rise and Fall of the Wang Regime
ch15.note: Wang zhengquan de kaichang yu shouchang: a history of the Wang Jingwei government by the journalist Jin Xiongbai, writing under the pen name Zhu Zijia. A real work, serialized from 1959 in the Hong Kong magazine Chunqiu and later issued in six volumes; it gives the fullest account from the Wang side, which Chen here quotes and corrects.

ch15.anchor: An Account of the Conduct of Mr. Zeng Zhongming
ch15.note: A xingzhuang is a traditional account of the conduct and career of a person newly dead, drawn up to supply the materials for a formal biography or epitaph. Wang Jingwei composed one for Zeng Zhongming, the aide killed in his place at Hanoi; Zeng, gravely wounded, is said to have died after signing over the funds held in his name and losing too much blood.

Ju yi ge li: a long public statement Wang Jingwei issued on 9 April 1939 defending his call for peace with Japan, in which he cited the record of a wartime meeting of the Supreme National Defense Council. Chen and his contemporaries charged that Wang had tampered with that record; the piece is a real document of the propaganda war that followed the Hanoi attempt.

Wu Jingheng (1865-1953), better known by his courtesy name Zhihui, a revered elder of the Nationalist Party, classical scholar and calligrapher, and one of its senior moral authorities; he had earlier drafted the resolution expelling Wang from the Party. His rejoinder to 'To Cite One Instance' was among the most cutting of the replies to Wang.

ch15.anchor: the new Hiranuma cabinet in Japan
ch15.note: The cabinet of Baron Hiranuma Kiichiro, Japanese prime minister from January to August 1939, which succeeded Konoe's. Its comparative coolness toward Wang left him, for a time, stranded and uncertain of Japanese backing.

ch15.anchor: the guilt reaches not to wife and child
ch15.note: An old principle of Chinese law and morals, that punishment for a crime should not reach a man's wife and children. Chen invokes it to spare the household; the bitter irony is that the raid killed Zeng Zhongming and wounded his wife and several of Wang's people, while Wang himself went unharmed.
